UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
POST-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF  
GERONIMO POWER, LLC 
 
Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or the “Commission”) 
July 30, 2026 Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment,1 Geronimo Power, LLC (“Geronimo 
Power”) hereby submits these comments urging PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and the 
Commission to adopt reforms to the PJM stakeholder process and governance structure that ensure 
PJM’s independence and provide PJM with the tools necessary to administer its markets and 
effectively respond to regional challenges. 
I. 
COMMENTS 
The Commission has long recognized that “the success of [Regional Transmission 
Organizations (“RTOs”)] will depend on both the perception and reality of [their] independence.”2  
Indeed, FERC has explained that “the principle of independence is the bedrock upon which the 
[Independent System Operator (“ISO”)] must be built.”3  For an RTO or ISO to achieve 
independence consistent with this bedrock principle, FERC requires that they possess certain core 
characteristics.  These characteristics include a “decisionmaking process that is independent of 
 
1 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Docket No. AD26-7-000, Notice Requesting Post-Conference 
Comment (July 30, 2026).  
2 Reg’l Transmission Orgs., Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089, 65 Fed. Reg. 809 at 855, 89 
FERC ¶ 61,285 (1999) (“Order No. 2000”), order on reh’g, Order No. 2000-A, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,092, 90 
FERC ¶ 61,201 (2000), aff’d sub nom. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Snohomish Cnty., Wash. v. FERC, 272 F.3d 607 (D.C. 
Cir. 2001). 
3 Order No. 2000, 65 Fed. Reg. at 842.  See also Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 4 (D.C. Cir. 2002) 
(“The Commission emphasized that an ISO’s independence with respect to governance and financial interests was 
fundamental to assuring that an ISO would not favor any class of transmission users.”).

2 
 
control by any market participant or class of participants” given “that the independence of an RTO 
ultimately depends on who makes the decisions.”4  The Commission also requires that “RTOs, in 
order to ensure their independence from market participants, must have the independent and 
exclusive right to make section 205 filings that apply to the rates, terms and conditions of 
transmission services over the facilities operated by the RTO.”5  
While PJM and its board have been structured to be independent of market participants, 
experience has shown that the structure of the PJM stakeholder process is impairing the ability of 
PJM to act independently and effectively to advance policies that it views as serving the needs of 
the region.  The existing governance structure has resulted in a stakeholder process that is 
susceptible to gridlock and that can prevent proposed solutions to pressing market issues from 
moving forward through the process.  Additionally, the existing board structure can create 
disincentives for board members to vote for proposals that may not align with the interests of 
certain stakeholders to avoid adversely affecting their reelection prospects.  These issues are 
compounded by the fact that PJM does not enjoy the full suite of filing rights that public utilities 
have historically been entitled to under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”). 
These aspects of PJM’s stakeholder process and governance structure are not new.  But the 
significant challenges that PJM has faced in recent years have exposed the shortcomings of the 
existing stakeholder process and governance model.  PJM itself has observed that “[t]he PJM 
region is now navigating a convergence of three structural forces that have pushed the system into 
 
4 Order No. 2000, 65 Fed. Reg. at 854.  See also 18 C.F.R. § 35.34(j)(1)(ii) (“The Regional Transmission 
Organization must have a decision making process that is independent of control by any market participant or class of 
participants.”).  
5 Order No. 2000, 65 Fed. Reg. at 858.  See also 18 C.F.R. § 35.34(j)(1)(iii) (“The Regional Transmission 
Organization must have exclusive and independent authority under section 205 of the Federal Power Act (16 U.S.C. 
824d), to propose rates, terms and conditions of transmission service provided over the facilities it operates.”).

3 
 
disequilibrium.”6  These forces include a supply shortage that has resulted in the last two PJM 
Base Residual Auctions clearing over 6,000 MW short of PJM’s RTO-wide reliability 
requirement7 and an “urgent need to bring new Capacity Resources online quickly to serve the 
remarkable load growth in the PJM Region.”8   
If PJM is going to address these and other challenges, the PJM stakeholder process and 
governance framework must be reformed to ensure that PJM can take decisive action to address 
pressing market design issues while ensuring accountability for market outcomes.  As discussed 
in more detail below and in Geronimo Power’s responses to the issue list developed by the 
Commission and attached hereto as Attachment A, Geronimo Power believes that the PJM 
governing documents and manuals should be modified in a manner that ensures that PJM is able 
to move its preferred proposals efficiently through the stakeholder process—with advisory input 
from stakeholders and state authorities—and provides PJM with the Section 205 filing rights 
required to allow it to pursue necessary changes.  
Geronimo Power also believes that board member terms should be modified to further 
insulate board members from political pressure, provide them with greater autonomy to exercise 
independent judgment, and allow the board to pursue policies needed to advance the interests of 
the region.  Extending the standard terms of PJM board members to five years and establishing a 
two-term limit will both (1) provide board members with greater latitude to vote in a manner that 
they believe aligns with the interests of the region as a whole without concern for their reelection 
 
6 PJM, Powering Reliability Through Market Design: Addressing Rising Demand and Constrained Supply, 
and Stimulating Investment To Support Durable Reliability at 4 (May 6, 2026), available at: https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-
design.pdf?_sp=cab50bb7-7325-471c-a9ba-7eeed5235c22.1786828904496. 
7 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address 
Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from New Load Adjustments at 7-8 (July 31, 2026). 
8 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-1563-000, Proposed Tariff Amendments for Expedited 
Interconnection Track at 3 (Feb. 27, 2026).

4 
 
prospects or fear of retribution and (2) ensure the PJM board benefits from the infusion of new 
talent and perspectives while also mitigating the potential for undue influence that can accompany 
unlimited re-election to the board.      
A. 
PJM’s Stakeholder Process Must Be Reformed  
 
PJM’s current reliance on a consensus-driven stakeholder process in which multiple 
committees and subcommittees develop, modify, and ultimately approve (or disapprove) of 
proposals is impairing the ability of PJM to move decisively to address market design issues and 
ensure reliability for the PJM region.9  Under the existing framework, an individual proposal often 
is required to navigate layers of committee and task force review before a proposal reaches the 
senior committees and, ultimately, the board.10  New initiatives, regardless of their importance or 
the timeline upon which they should be addressed, must generally proceed from an issue charge, 
through task force or subcommittee deliberations, to standing committee review, before receiving 
votes from the Markets and Reliability Committee and Members Committee.11  Throughout these 
stages, stakeholders are encouraged to resolve their differences and develop consensus packages, 
with proposals often requiring majority or supermajority support before a proposal can advance.12  
The existing consensus-based approach ensures that all stakeholders can provide input on 
relevant proposals and register their objections.  But it also creates opportunities for delay, 
procedural disputes, the preservation of the status quo, and results in compromise policies that too 
often fall short of what is necessary to address critical market design issues.  The result is that the 
 
9 PJM Manual 34: PJM Stakeholder Process § 8 (Revision 22; effective Sept. 25, 2025). 
10 Id. 
11 Id. § 8 and App. III. 
12 Id. § 8.3 (“The goal of the Standing Committees is to reach as much agreement as possible on a single 
proposal, unless the Senior Standing Committee requests multiple options.”);  id. § 7.4 (“The goal is to reach as much 
agreement on as many elements of the issue as possible, where consensus is defined as unanimity – where all 
consenting parties can accept or will not object to the proposed solution.”).

5 
 
proposal that ultimately emerges from this process—to the extent it is not effectively blocked by 
a coalition of Members—may be a stakeholder compromise rather than the solution that best 
advances market operations and reliability.  While this stakeholder process may have been 
appropriate when PJM functioned principally as a power pool and the region’s needs were less 
diverse, it is increasingly ill-suited to an RTO responsible for administering complex regional 
markets and addressing rapidly evolving reliability and market-design challenges. 
Geronimo Power believes that PJM, as a public utility and the independent entity charged 
with administering its markets, should take responsibility for determining which issues warrant 
action and for developing the proposals that it believes best advance reliability, competitive market 
outcomes, and the interests of the region as a whole in consultation with stakeholders and the 
states. Geronimo Power also believes that the multi-layered committee review and voting 
procedures that characterize the current PJM stakeholder process can no longer be permitted to 
delay proposals that PJM seeks to implement on a more expedited timeline.  PJM must have the 
ability to timely implement proposals that it believes will best address the region’s needs.   
PJM should establish and manage a transparent, time-limited, proposal-development 
process for significant market-design initiatives.  Each year, PJM should establish a work plan 
setting out the initiatives that it believes should be pursued in the upcoming year, establishing the 
scope and objective of each stakeholder initiative, and setting a time frame for the development 
and implementation of proposals.13  This workplan should be established in coordination with 
stakeholders with a designated timeframe for stakeholders to comment on the workplan and offer 
 
13 Although PJM should have the flexibility necessary to modify the timeline for stakeholder initiatives as 
necessary to account for issues that may arise during the policy development process, PJM should endeavor to stick 
to the timelines established in the workplan.  If it is unable to do so, then it should be required to provide an explanation 
to stakeholders and the board of why such timelines were not met and outline its plan to complete the initiative within 
a reasonable period of time.

6 
 
ideas of other initiatives that PJM should pursue.  Once a final workplan is established, PJM should 
take the lead in driving the relevant stakeholder processes forward, including developing any initial 
scoping materials or proposals, publishing relevant data and analyses, and soliciting, evaluating, 
and incorporating stakeholder feedback.  After considering relevant stakeholder input, PJM would 
publish a revised proposal and ultimately a final staff recommendation to the PJM board explaining 
the basis for its proposed approach, why it will better address market needs than relevant 
alternatives, and its response to stakeholder concerns.    
Other RTOs/ISOs have adopted similar structures.  For instance, the California 
Independent System Operator Corporation (“CAISO”) has adopted a stakeholder process in which 
CAISO staff has primary responsibility for working with stakeholders to identify issues of concern, 
establishing a timeline for addressing relevant issues, and driving necessary market design changes 
forward through the stakeholder process.  Each year CAISO staff uses its market policy catalog 
and roadmap process to solicit proposed initiatives from stakeholders, assess stakeholder support 
for taking up matters in the stakeholder process, determine the relative priority of various 
initiatives, and establishing a workplan and timeline for moving forward with the development 
and implementation of necessary market design changes.14  Once an initiative is added to the 
stakeholder roadmap, it enters the proposal development process based on its priority, with CAISO 
staff taking the lead in publishing issue papers and proposals, leading stakeholder discussions, and 
ultimately crafting a final proposal for presentation to the CAISO board.  Throughout the process, 
stakeholders can provide written comments, participate in stakeholder meetings, exchange 
information with the CAISO and other stakeholders, and discuss proposed market design 
 
14 CAISO, Stakeholder Process: A Guide for Stakeholders to engage and participate in policy development 
at the California ISO at 4 (Dec. 2025), available at: https://www.caiso.com/library/stakeholder-center.

7 
 
changes.15 
While shifting to a framework where PJM staff has responsibility for driving proposals 
forward would streamline the existing stakeholder process and place more responsibility on PJM, 
stakeholders must continue to have the opportunity to provide meaningful input on proposals prior 
to when they are submitted to the PJM board and the Commission for review.  Indeed, Geronimo 
Power agrees with the sentiment expressed at the Commission’s technical conference and in many 
of the comments filed in this proceeding that a strength of PJM’s stakeholder process is that it 
ensures that a broad range of market participants and stakeholders are able to provide input on 
proposed reforms.  Geronimo Power also agrees that allowing PJM states to fully participate in 
debates among PJM stakeholders and to provide PJM with critical information related to how 
proposals under consideration may affect their citizens is beneficial.   
 
For that reason, Geronimo Power believes that stakeholders must continue to have the 
opportunity to provide input on what issues are pursued through the stakeholder process and on 
proposals crafted by PJM staff through participation in stakeholder meetings, written comments, 
and advisory votes.  Specifically:  
• Members and other stakeholders, including the states, should be afforded the opportunity 
to submit written comments on PJM’s proposals as they are vetted through the stakeholder 
process.  To promote transparency, stakeholder comments should be posted publicly.  
Additionally, PJM staff should have an obligation to provide a response to stakeholder 
comments.  While an individual stakeholder-by-stakeholder response may not be 
necessary, PJM should be required to respond to the substance of stakeholder concerns so 
that stakeholders and the PJM board can understand how PJM accounted for stakeholder 
input, including why PJM elected not to pursue relevant alternatives offered by 
stakeholders. 
• PJM should have the ability to determine what committees, subcommittees, or working 
groups a proposal is assigned, including discretion to have a proposal go directly to a 
standing committee, the Markets & Reliability Committee, or the Members Committee.  
PJM’s existing stakeholder process often results in proposals being delayed as they 
 
15 Id. at 5-6.

8 
 
progress through multiple levels of working group, subcommittee, and committee review.  
Yet these multiple levels of review are not always necessary for the development of a 
proposal.  This is particularly true when a proposal does not raise the sort of technical 
implementation issues that PJM’s working groups and subcommittees are often positioned 
to address.  Additionally, if PJM determines that the implementation of a proposal is time 
sensitive, it should have discretion to proceed immediately to the Markets & Reliability 
Committee or the Members Committee.  
• Members should continue to have the opportunity to vote on proposals that proceed through 
the existing committee structure.  However, these votes should be advisory in nature rather 
than determinative of whether a proposal advances or not.  While PJM should have the 
discretion to make modifications to its proposal to account for the results of a vote, the 
results of any vote should not determine whether a proposal moves forward.  
• The record developed in the course of the stakeholder proceeding, including any written 
comments, the results of stakeholder votes, sector-specific positions, and relevant 
alternative proposals should accompany any recommendation that PJM provides to its 
board—who would act as the ultimate decision-maker on whether a filing is made with 
FERC—to ensure that the board has a transparent record of both PJM’s proposed solution 
and the degree and nature of stakeholder support or opposition.   
Such a structure would preserve the benefits of robust stakeholder participation while recognizing 
that responsibility for the timely and independent administration of the PJM markets ultimately 
rests with PJM and the board. 
Reorienting the PJM stakeholder process from a consensus-driven decision-making 
structure to an advisory structure would preserve transparency and stakeholder participation while 
reducing procedural obstacles that impede timely action.  The PJM board would continue to serve 
as the ultimate decision maker, informed by PJM’s recommendations and stakeholder input, but 
regional reforms would no longer depend upon a prolonged process that requires obtaining 
successive committee approvals before meaningful action can occur.  And to the extent that 
stakeholders are concerned that such an advisory role may prove insufficient, they would still have 
the rights afforded to them under the FPA to express their support or opposition to a given PJM

9 
 
proposal in front of the Commission through comments, protests, or complaints.16    
B. 
PJM Should Have All FPA Section 205 Filing Rights Necessary For It To 
Administer Its Markets And Plan And Operate Its System 
1. 
PJM’s Section 205 Rights Should Be Expanded To Allow It To Make 
Section 205 Filings Respecting The Tariffs That It Administers 
Section 205 of the FPA reflects Congress’s determination that public utilities—not FERC 
or other third parties—should have the unilateral right to propose changes to the rates, terms, and 
conditions of service that it provides.  As the courts have explained, “Section 205 of the Federal 
Power Act gives a utility the right to file rates and terms for services rendered with its assets.”17  If 
FERC or other third parties wish to make changes to the rates, terms, and conditions of service, 
then they are required to make a filing under Section 206 of the FPA demonstrating that the existing 
rate is unjust and unreasonable and the proposed alternative is just and reasonable.18   
 
The allocation of Section 205 filing rights in PJM has strayed from this statutory scheme.  
In PJM, Section 205 filing rights are divided between PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners 
Committee depending on the governing document and subject matter.  PJM generally has the right 
to make Section 205 filings proposing changes to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) 
or the Reliability Assurance Agreement (“RAA”),19 while the PJM Transmission Owners retain 
exclusive rights over transmission revenue requirements, regional transmission rate design, and 
recovery of transmission-related costs.20  Additionally, PJM’s ability to make a Section 205 filing 
respecting the Operating Agreement is conditioned upon approval by a super-majority vote of the 
 
16 More specific information regarding Geronimo Power’s proposed reforms to the PJM stakeholder process 
are included in Geronimo Power’s responses to the issue list developed by the Commission and attached hereto as 
Attachment A. 
17 Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 9 (D.C. Cir. 2002). 
18 PJM Power Providers Grp. v. FERC, 88 F.4th 250, 259 (3rd Cir. 2023). 
19 PJM OATT § 9.2. 
20 Id. § 9.1(a).

10 
 
Members Committee.21  The result, as Deputy Secretary of Energy James Danly observed in his 
opening remarks at the Commission’s technical conference, is a situation where responsibility for 
ensuring that the PJM markets operate effectively is dispersed among multiple actors and bodies 
and it is “unclear who it is that’s responsible for what.”22 
 
PJM should be responsible for market outcomes and should have the filing rights under 
Section 205 of the FPA necessary to propose tariff revisions that it believes are required to maintain 
the efficiency and reliability of the PJM markets.  This includes being permitted to file revisions 
to the operating, planning, and markets rules in the Operating Agreement, including unilateral 
changes to Schedule No. 1 (PJM Interchange Energy Market), Schedule No. 2 (Component of 
Cost), and Schedule No. 6 (Regional Transmission Expansion Planning Protocol), without any 
obligation to obtain approval from stakeholders.  
 
Indeed, if PJM’s FPA Section 205 filing rights remain constrained, the stakeholder reforms 
discussed above may be of limited effect.  After all, a PJM-driven stakeholder process in which 
stakeholders and states play an advisory role will have little benefit if PJM is unable to file its 
preferred reform to the Operating Agreement unless it has obtained the requisite support from 
stakeholders.  PJM should be granted the FPA Section 205 rights necessary for it to present its 
preferred reforms, regardless of stakeholder approval, to the Commission.  
2. 
FERC Should Reject Requests To Give States FPA Section 205 Rights 
Granting states Section 205 filing rights would be inconsistent with the FPA, whether these 
rights are exercised directly by the state regulator or indirectly by compelling PJM to file a state’s 
preferred rates, terms, and conditions of service with FERC.  Section 205 authorizes a public 
 
21 PJM Operating Agreement § 8.4(c). 
22 FERC, Commission-Led Technical Conference on PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms (July 23, 
2026) (Opening statement of Dep. Sec. of Energy J. Danly at 41:58), available at: https://www.ferc.gov/news-
events/events/PJM-Governance-Stakeholder-Reforms.

11 
 
utility—and no other entity—to make filings respecting its rates, terms, and conditions of service.23  
Section 205 of the FPA “governs changes that the utility itself proposes, not those that a state 
regulator requires it to propose.”24  Allowing states to compel a utility to make Section 205 filings 
would be inconsistent “with the purposes of the entire procedural scheme.”25   
 
Indeed, providing states Section 205 filing rights would be inconsistent with the limitations 
established on FERC’s authority by Congress.  Section 201 of the FPA explicitly exempts states 
and political subdivisions of the state from FERC jurisdiction.  As the courts have recognized, the 
“structure of the Federal Power Act clearly reflects Congress’s intent to exempt governmental 
entities from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s” authority.26  Even if PJM were 
inclined to delegate filing authority to state regulators, placing FERC in the position of passing 
judgment on rates, terms, and conditions proposed by state actors under Section 205 of the FPA is 
inconsistent with the intent of Congress and the plain language of the FPA.  
There also is no compelling reason that states need to be granted Section 205 rights, as 
Congress already has granted them ample opportunities to ensure that their views are considered 
by the Commission.  States can intervene27 in proceedings concerning PJM and lodge protests (or 
supporting comments) in response to filings with FERC.  Moreover, if a state views an existing 
tariff provision as unjust, unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory or preferential, it can file a 
complaint with the Commission under FPA Section 206 and, if successful, require the utility to 
revise such provision.   
 
23 16 U.S.C. § 824d(c) (authorizing a “public utility” to make filings respecting the rates, terms, and 
conditions of FERC-jurisdictional service). 
24 Mass DPU v. FERC, 729 F.2d 886, 887 (1st Cir. 1984).   
25 Id. at 888.   
26 Transmission Agency of N. Cal. v. FERC, 495 F.3d 663, 673 (D.C. Cir. 2007). 
27 In fact, any state commission automatically becomes a party to a proceeding after timely filing a notice of 
intervention in such proceeding.  18 C.F.R. § 385.214(a)(2).

12 
 
To be clear, Geronimo Power believes that states have an important perspective that should, 
as discussed above, be considered as part of a PJM-driven stakeholder process.  But elevating 
states in a manner that allows them to dictate the Section 205 filings made by PJM is incompatible 
with the statutory scheme enacted by Congress.  And, as courts have recognized, elevating the role 
of states in a multi-state region like PJM so that they have effective FPA section 205 filing rights 
“threatens confusion, possibly chaos” when different states seek to impose different filing demands 
on PJM.28  To the extent states want to pursue options that differ from PJM’s preferred approach, 
they have ample opportunity to express these views through existing PJM functions (e.g. the PJM 
state relations function), by participating in stakeholder meetings and by making filings with 
FERC.  These avenues, however, must remain consistent with the framework of the FPA and ensure 
that PJM, as the entity ultimately responsible for operating efficient markets and maintaining a 
reliable system, has Section 205 filings rights that allow it to carry out its core operations, planning 
and market functions.  
C. 
PJM Board Service Should Be Limited To Two, Five-Year Terms 
Geronimo Power believes that the existing framework for electing members of the PJM 
board—coupled with their three-year terms—creates a disincentive for board members to make 
decisions that have the potential to trigger opposition from certain constituencies within the region.  
Since board members are nominated by a committee of PJM Members and must be approved by 
the Members Committee, board members have a keen understanding of how their votes, 
particularly when their term is near expiration, may affect their chances to be re-elected to the 
board.  This structure has the potential to undermine independent decision-making in a manner 
that is in tension with the independence that is at the core of PJM’s mandate.    
 
28 Mass DPU v. FERC, 729 F.2d 886, 888 (1st Cir. 1984).

13 
 
The terms of PJM board members should be modified to mitigate the risk of political 
pressure and provide board members with greater flexibility to take the actions necessary to serve 
the interests of the region as a whole.  PJM board members currently serve three-year terms.29  
These short three-year terms leave board members that would like to serve longer than three years 
in a politically sensitive position knowing that any decision they make upon taking their board seat 
may be held against them by the PJM Nominating Committee or Members Committee if they seek 
reappointment.  This issue is compounded by the rules allowing board members to be reappointed 
for additional terms without limit and also risks the entrenchment of such board members with 
particular interests or perspectives that may not always align with the needs of PJM. 
Geronimo Power urges PJM and the Commission to extend the term of PJM board 
members to five years and limit the ability of board members to serve an additional term to a single 
additional term.  Establishing a five-year term for PJM board members will further insulate board 
members from political pressure and provide these individuals with greater latitude to vote for 
those proposals that they believe align with the longer-term needs of the region.  Moreover, 
providing board members with the ability to seek only one additional term will better ensure that 
board members retain their independence and that fresh perspectives are regularly introduced to 
the board.30  A board member that may only seek reappointment one-time at the conclusion of a 
five-year term will have more independence to cast votes based solely on what is best for the PJM 
region as a whole than board members that can seek continual reappointment following short three-
year terms.  
 
29 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.3(b). 
30 More specific information regarding the reforms Geronimo Power believes should be implemented to 
ensure the PJM board’s independence is included in Geronimo Power’s responses to the issue list developed by the 
Commission and attached hereto as Attachment A.

14 
 
II.  
CONCLUSION 
Geronimo Power respectfully requests that the Commission take actions consistent with its 
filings in this proceeding.  
Respectfully submitted, 
 
  /s/ Matthew Morais

6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes 
be made public or the Board be required to explain 
its reasoning? 
X 
 
Yes, Board votes should be public and the 
Board should state its reasoning for accepting 
or rejecting proposals advanced by PJM, 
including discussing relevant alternatives and 
stakeholder views at a level sufficient to show 
that they were considered. 
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board 
meetings be open or available to the public? 
X 
 
Yes, for portions dealing with policy direction 
and stakeholder matters. Executive session

Question 
Yes 
No 
Comment 
should be preserved for personnel, litigation, 
market-sensitive and CEII matters.  
8) 
Should PJM's governing documents be revised to 
explicitly state that the responsibility of PJM and its 
Board is to serve the public interest? 
 
X 
PJM's mandate is already defined by function: 
reliable and safe delivery of energy at the most 
efficient price.  
An open-ended public interest principle is a 
standard that is not capable of being 
meaningfully implemented. Across a footprint 
of thirteen states and D.C. it would be 
construed differently in each jurisdiction and 
could result in PJM being held to varying 
operational 
and 
market 
performance 
requirements and/or benchmarks unrelated to 
the ISO core functions and associated 
outcomes. Where the states are aligned the 
language adds nothing; where they are not it 
becomes a lever for whichever coalition is 
assembled at the time. PJM and the Board 
should answer to an objective standard focused 
on the efficiency and effectiveness of its core 
functions – markets, operations, and planning. 
 
The concern applies with greater force to 
affordability. Affordability is a legitimate 
objective that PJM serves through efficient 
dispatch, 
competitive 
procurement, 
and 
disciplined planning, but as a governing 
principle it can be used as a justification for 
suppressing price levels in a manner that 
undermines competitive markets, mutes long-
term price signals, raises the cost of capital for 
new supply, undermines resource adequacy, 
and increases costs to consumers in the long-
term. 
9) 
Should state representatives have at least one voting 
member on the Nominating Committee? 
 
X 
No.  A state-selected voting seat introduces an 
additional political element 
into Board 
composition. 
 
No 
single 
state-selected 
representative can be expected to speak for 
thirteen states and the District of Columbia on 
all matters.  
10) 
Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and 
tie management compensation to their achievement? 
X 
 
Compensation should be administered by the 
Board within its sole discretion in terms of 
both the scope of the metrics, the related 
achievement 
benchmarks 
and 
their 
accompanying 
compensation 
impact.  
Compensation should also be weighted toward 
outcomes 
PJM 
controls 
such 
as 
interconnection throughput, planning cycle 
time, operational performance, and timeliness 
of filings. Compensation should not be tied to 
achieving particular price levels, which would 
encourage 
operator 
intervention 
and 
undermine market integrity.

Question 
Yes 
No 
Comment 
 
Geronimo supports public metrics and public 
reporting of performance. Geronimo does not 
believe that the compensation of individual 
PJM employees need to be published.    
Section 205 Filing Rights 
 
Questions / Comments 
Yes 
No 
Comments 
11) 
Should the stakeholder process be advisory, i.e., 
stakeholder votes only inform the Board? 
X 
 
Yes.  PJM must have the right to make 
unilateral Section 205 filings respecting core 
RTO functions such as planning, markets, and 
operations.  
 
An advisory role does not mean that PJM 
should be free to disregard stakeholder input, 
but the obligation on the Board to consider 
stakeholder advice should be modeled on an 
administrative rulemaking process where 
parties can submit comments, but the agency 
(or in this case PJM) ultimately decides. PJM 
should be required to respond to stakeholder 
comments, but should retain control over 
whether a proposal moves forward through the 
stakeholder process.  Similarly, when the 
Board makes a decision it should publish the 
reasons for its decision, including addressing 
the positions of stakeholders at a high level. 
This is similar to the process the Commission 
follows in a rulemaking. 
 
Stakeholders that believe that a market rule 
needs to be changed will retain their rights 
under Section 206 to file a complaint with 
FERC. 
12) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over the 
energy market and ancillary services unencumbered 
by the requirement to obtain approval of two-thirds 
of the Members Committee? 
X 
 
PJM must have authority over the core RTO 
functions of planning, markets, and operations, 
including the ability to make Section 205 
filings concerning these matters. Geronimo 
also supports relocating Operating Agreement 
Schedules 1 (PJM Interchange Energy Market) 
and 2 (Component of Cost) to the Tariff (and 
Schedule 6 as discussed further below).  As the 
utility responsible for administering its 
markets, PJM should have the right to make 
Section 205 filings without being obligated to 
obtain approval of two-thirds of the Members 
Committee.  
13) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over 
Regional Transmission Expansion Planning (RTEP) 
unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval 
of two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
X 
 
PJM is an outlier among RTOs in lacking filing 
authority over its own regional planning 
protocol. As stated above, PJM must have 
authority over the core RTO functions of

Questions / Comments 
Yes 
No 
Comments 
planning, markets, and operations, including 
the ability to make Section 205 filings related 
to the Regional Transmission Expansion 
Protocol. 
 
 
14) 
Should OPSI have “jump ball” rights over resource 
adequacy and transmission cost allocation filings 
when a supermajority of OPSI agrees on an 
alternative proposal? 
 
X 
No.  The FPA already provides states with the 
ability to seek to reform tariff rules through a 
Section 206 complaint. There is no need to 
grant states any rights to compel PJM to submit 
states’ preferred proposal to FERC under 
Section 205 of the FPA. States also retain their 
own authority over siting, procurement, retail 
policy, and large-load tariffs.  Additionally, 
states also have the ability to support the 
construction of new transmission through the 
state agreement approach.   
 
The goal of this proceeding should be to 
increase the efficiency and effectiveness of the 
stakeholder and governance process in PJM.  
Creating a host of new entities with filing or 
“jump ball” rights is contrary to that objective. 
 
15) 
Should the Members Committee have “jump ball” 
filing rights over the portions of the tariff where PJM 
has 205 filing rights when a supermajority of 
stakeholders approves an alternative proposal? 
 
X 
No.  The FPA already provides members with 
the ability to seek to reform tariff rules through 
a Section 206 complaint.  There is no need to 
grant members any rights to compel PJM to 
submit their preferred proposal to FERC under 
Section 205 of the FPA.  Stakeholders also 
have the right to submit comments on 
proposals as they work their way through the 
stakeholder process and when filings are 
submitted to FERC under Section 205 of the 
FPA.  
 
Granting new “jump ball” rights will only add 
further complexity and chaos into the PJM 
governance framework. PJM is responsible for 
administering its markets; there is no 
compelling reason for a “jump ball” filing right 
for stakeholders. Geronimo encourages the 
Commission to pursue reforms through this 
proceeding that streamline the stakeholder 
process rather than creating a host of new filing 
and jump ball rights for stakeholders and the 
states.  
 
The goal of this proceeding should be to 
increase the efficiency and effectiveness of the 
stakeholder and governance process in PJM.  
Creating a host of new entities with filing or 
“jump ball” rights is contrary to that objective.

16) 
Should the approval threshold in the Members 
Committee be lowered from two-thirds sector-
weighted voting? 
X 
 
If the stakeholder vote is not advisory as 
Geronimo recommends, a lower threshold 
should be established since it makes it more 
likely that PJM’s proposals will move forward 
and not be vetoed by a minority of 
stakeholders, which increases the risk of undue 
influence and delay. 
 
Geronimo's first preference is that the vote be 
advisory 
(Question 
11). 
Lowering 
the 
threshold, and reconsidering sector weighting, 
are the appropriate secondary reforms if the 
vote remains binding. 
17) 
Should the voting rules barring affiliate votes, which 
apply to senior standing committees, also apply to 
lower-level committees? 
X 
 
The disparity between lower and senior 
committee voting rules invites positioning at 
the level where it is least visible and produces 
inconsistent signals as an issue moves upward. 
Making stakeholder voting advisory would 
address this issue. 
 
If stakeholder voting is not made advisory, 
Geronimo supports aligning the manner of 
voting at standing committees with the 
Members Committee, and permitting disclosed 
proxy voting subject to the same affiliate 
restrictions.

18) 
In addition to OPSI, should there be a second state 
representative group consisting of governors' 
representatives 
and/or 
state 
legislators' 
representatives? 
 
X 
OPSI represents an important voice. State 
commissions play an important role in the 
actual substantive matters that impact core ISO 
functions – e.g. siting, procurement, permitting 
of generation, large-load interconnection, and 
numerous other policies. Another organization 
devoted to governors’ representatives and/or 
state legislators’ representatives is unnecessary 
because to the extent those bodies/forums have 
positions on the substantive ISO functions 
their respective utility commissions are best 
suited to communicate those positions to the 
ISO.   
 
State commissions are capable of consulting 
their governors' offices and legislatures and 
representing those positions in OPSI.  PJM

also already maintains a well-developed state 
relations 
function. 
OPSI 
and 
state 
commissions are also well positioned to 
represent their states’ interests in front of 
FERC, where the executive and legislative 
branches of the states are also free to 
participate.  
19) 
Should state representatives have a formal voting 
role in the stakeholder process (limited to certain 
topics, such as resource adequacy and regional 
transmission cost allocation) in addition to the 
consumer advocate votes? 
X 
 
Yes, BUT any vote should be advisory only 
and the nature of the vote cast should be 
transparent to other stakeholders.   
 
 
20) 
Should PJM be required to consult with OPSI prior 
to making a section 205 filing related to resource 
adequacy and transmission cost allocation? 
 
X 
PJM makes filings at a volume that a general 
consultation obligation would be impracticable 
and slow down the process.  OPSI should be 
permitted to provide input through the 
stakeholder process, which provides more than 
adequate process to understand and provide 
input on any issue.
